title: UK launch flood taskforce to prepare for extreme winter weather
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter.

After a summer of record-breaking temperatures, the group will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for what the Met Office described as the "heightened potential" for wet, windy, stormy weather in the coming months.

"We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting.

The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.

Flooding and drought are devolved areas for Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales but Defra says the devolved governments will still be part of the UK-wide taskforce, which will aim to bring together expertise and share information.

Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, gathering the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries.

Hardy said: "This will put communities and businesses at the heart of our work and will make sure the UK is ready for whatever the weather brings next."

The government has committed at least £10.5bn until 2036 to protect homes, businesses and critical infrastructure from the growing threat of flooding.

The Met Office has said the current seasonal outlook suggests an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions during autumn, in part due to the El Niño weather event.

It has warned that this year's iteration of the climate phenomenon is likely to be the strongest in living memory, with the peak not expected until the end of the year.

The Environment Agency has said that while flooding is not guaranteed, the odds of repeated storms, prolonged rain and saturated catchments are higher than average this winter.

It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.

The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record.

Last winter brought four named storms to the UK - Bram, Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra - and several significant flooding events, with the Met Office reporting that England received 42% more rainfall than its winter average.

Clarification 15 October: This article has been updated to explain that flooding and drought are devolved areas but that Defra has said devolved governments will still be part of the UK-wide taskforce.

title: Tropical Storm Isaias Set to Be First Atlantic Hurricane of 2026 Season
author: Brian Kahn
content:
The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has been mercifully dull, but that’s set to change this week. Tropical Storm Isaias is forecast to become the season’s first hurricane before making landfall somewhere between Mississippi and Florida by the weekend.

El Niño has turned the Atlantic basin into a graveyard by changing winds high in the atmosphere so that they rip apart storms. That’s helped depress tropical cyclone activity to near-record-low levels and resulted in zero hurricanes. That could change imminently, though.

Isaias is churning in the Gulf of Mexico with winds of 65 mph, according to the latest update from the US National Hurricane Center. That’s just a shade below hurricane strength. The storm is forecast to pass over a patch of abnormally warm water, providing fuel for it to blossom into a hurricane. It could peak as a Category 2 storm with winds of 110 mph as it lumbers to the northeast. The storm is expected to weaken due to those aforementioned gnarly winds shortly before it makes landfall somewhere along the Gulf Coast.

The NHC has issued hurricane watches for all the coastline in Mississippi and Alabama as well as parts of the Florida Panhandle. (Tropical storm watches extend into Louisiana as well.)

Folks in that region can expect rainfall totals of up to 7 inches, though some spots in the Panhandle could see as much as 10 inches and storm surge as high as 7 feet. Tornadoes aren’t out of the question either. In other words, it’s a storm to take seriously.

Isaias could make also (or at least tie) history as the latest first Atlantic hurricane to form on record. The current record was set in 1905, when the season’s first hurricane formed on October 8. There’s still one more update scheduled for Isaias on Wednesday, so it’s possible it could just miss out on tying that mark.

Record or not, Isaias is indicative of the hurricane season that wasn’t. This year’s Atlantic hurricane season was forecast to be below average. But it’s been even quieter than expected owing to an El Niño that’s been dubbed “super,” “Godzilla,” and “supersized.” The superlatives—which meteorologists will be quick to tell you are not official designations—are indicative of the strength of this year’s event. El Niño is measured by ocean temperatures in a part of the tropical Pacific, and this year’s iteration has seen record highs throughout the summer and first part of fall.

The intensity has had a heavy hand in rearranging the atmosphere around the world, including over the Atlantic. Saharan dust has also played a role in quieting things by making the air in one of the major areas where hurricanes develop too damn dry.

For a sense of how that has impacted the Atlantic hurricane season, we can look at some averages. From 1991 to 2020, the basin saw an average of 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes—that is, storms of Category 3 or greater—annually, according to NHC data. This year has seen eight tropical storms and one soon-to-be hurricane.

Another metric to measure the season is accumulated cyclone energy (ACE for short), which takes into account not just the number and intensity of storms but how long they stick around. The ACE to date for 2026 is 10.8 units. The average for this time of year? Nearly 102, according to data maintained by Colorado State University. Most of that energy typically accumulates from mid-August through late September.

None of this is to say there might not be another surprise storm in the coming weeks. But with El Niño continuing to intensify and the peak of the season well past, the odds of this season seeing a sudden spurt of activity are minimal at best.

title: Why This Weekend’s Nor’easter Is Like a Hurricane
author: Dennis Mersereau
content:
A powerful nor’easter developing this week will bring wicked winds, rough surf, and heavy rains to coastal communities from North Carolina to Nova Scotia.

These types of storms are more synonymous with mid-winter than mid-fall. And true to form, this storm is a little different. It won’t drop snow or ice like a classic winter nor’easter. In fact, this system may bring a tease of tropical weather to an Atlantic basin that’s been devoid of hurricane activity so far this year.

An Impactful Nor’easter for the East Coast

Nor’easters are special types of low-pressure systems that earn their name from the fierce northeasterly winds that can lash coastlines.

The seed that’ll grow into this weekend’s nor’easter started developing on Wednesday a few hundred miles off North Carolina’s Outer Banks. The system will meander toward New England into this weekend before slowly winding down into early next week.

Forecasters expect strong, persistent winds to hit coastal locations from North Carolina to Nova Scotia. The strongest gusts will buffet New England through Friday and Saturday, when winds may reach 60 to 70 mph.

Communities throughout the region can expect coastal flooding, beach erosion, life-threatening rip currents, and dangerously rough surf. Isolated power outages are possible. Flight delays at New York's and Boston’s airports are also likely due to blustery winds and rain.

Computer models still don’t entirely agree on how close to the coast this storm will track, or how long it’ll linger in the area—both factors that are crucial to determining exact impacts. A slower track closer to the coast will plaster the region with stronger winds and heavier rainfall than a faster path or one that keeps the center of the storm farther out to sea.

Nor’easters Are Common in Late Fall and Winter

Nor’easters are most common between October and April as powerful jet streams sweep across North America. It’s unusual for such a potent nor’easter to develop this early in the season.

Nor’easters are considered non-tropical—or as meteorologists call them, extratropical—systems that typically draw most of their energy from intense upper-level winds. That’s different from hurricanes, which tend to feed on warmer-than-normal oceans. But low-pressure systems exist on a spectrum that sometimes makes it difficult to neatly define them as tropical or extratropical, and this storm is a prime example.

A Tropical Connection

Some computer models suggest that this week’s nor’easter may acquire some tropical characteristics as it intensifies off the Northeast coastline. Fully extratropical systems feature cold air throughout the entire core of the storm. This nor’easter, on the other hand, may briefly develop a shallow warm core, a phenomenon found in tropical storms and hurricanes. Cloud structure, the storm’s overall wind field, and thunderstorm activity near its center are other tropical characteristics to watch out for.

Even though it’s not likely to earn a name as a hurricane would, it’s important for residents throughout the region to pay attention to the threat of flooding, wind damage, and power outages.

It’s strangely fitting that a nor’easter may prove to be the most hurricane-like non-hurricane we’ve seen across the Atlantic basin this season. We’re now past the peak of hurricane season and the year remains historically quiet. Tropical activity here is running at less than 10 percent of normal for this point in the year. This is also the latest the season has gone without producing a hurricane since the satellite era began in 1966. A quiet hurricane season is a hallmark of an El Niño, when hot waters in the tropical Pacific create conditions in the atmosphere unsuitable for tropical storms to form in the Atlantic.

But winter is a different story, and this week’s storm is also a potential preview of what’s to come as El Niño gains strength. Strong El Niño events tend to influence an active storm track across the southern US during the cooler months, which may in turn lead to more coastal storms along the Eastern Seaboard.

title: Hurricane Polo's remnants bringing more rain to flood-struck U.S. Southwest
author: The Associated Press
content:
Hurricane Polo's remnants bringing more rain to flood-struck U.S. Southwest

toggle caption i Eduardo Verdugo/AP

PHOENIX — As former Hurricane Polo weakened over northwestern Mexico on Tuesday evening, the storm's remnants battered the U.S. Southwest, flooding roadways and forcing residents in small New Mexico towns to evacuate over concerns about a dam failing.

Polo had struck the Mexican state of Baja California Sur in the morning with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (177 kph). It crossed the Gulf of California and weakened to become a tropical storm as it moved inland to the northeast.

By Tuesday evening, the New Mexico Department of Transportation reported flooded roads and debris on highways across the state, while parts of Arizona had become especially drenched, leading to several water rescues.

That is after storms rolled through parts of the U.S. Southwest overnight Monday, saturating the ground, which can make flooding worse.

Sponsor Message

Later in the week, the flood risk is expected to move into parts of the central U.S., with heavy rain hitting Texas and Oklahoma beginning Tuesday night, according to the National Weather Service.

Southwest US sees heavy rains and floods

Bands of rain continued to sweep across the U.S. Southwest, causing desert rivers to surge and usually dry arroyos to rage with floodwater.

toggle caption i Eduardo Verdugo/AP

The potential failure of the dam in south central New Mexico prompted evacuations in three small communities with hundreds of residents along the Rio Grande. People in Rincon, Salem and Garfield were told to seek higher ground immediately "before conditions worsen." Residents were later told to evacuate from nearby Hatch, home to prized green chile crops, and farther north in Placitas.

Wide swaths of the U.S. Southwest were under flood watches as the complex system of tropical weather spread northeast from Mexico, with Polo as the main event.

"Definitely looking at the chances for urban flooding," weather service meteorologist Carter Greulich in Albuquerque said. "Don't drive through flooded roadways. Remain out of the arroyos, especially in our urban areas."

A person stranded on top of a vehicle in floodwaters west of Phoenix was rescued Tuesday morning. Video taken by Arizona Fire and Medical Services showed a helicopter lowering a rescuer to a person clinging to their overturned car. And in Zion National Park, in Utah, a helicopter rescued three people in Heaps Canyon after flash flooding hit.

Sponsor Message

North of Phoenix, a truck was swept away in a wash. The driver got out safely, Maricopa County sheriff's officials said.

The rocky, desert area typically gets less than 10 inches (25 centimeters) of rain annually with little vegetation to soak it up, making flash flooding a perpetual risk.

The Bureau of Land Management in Arizona also reported significant flooding and damage to access roads in a national conservation area and a sand dunes recreation area in the southeastern part of the state.

Back in Utah, the East Fork of the Virgin River near Zion raged with chocolate floodwater and a shipping container floated downstream.

In the small town of Orderville, Utah, where flooding began Monday night, Sabrina Dubay was driving home when her partner called and told her to stay away.

"The river came in and swept around the entirety of our house," Dubay said.

A camper, snowmobile trailer, and other items from Dubay's yard were swept away by the river. Neighbors and friends arrived to dig a trench around the house as the water rose around their home.

"It was coming in through our front doors," she said.

An unusually soggy September across the region set the stage: When the ground is saturated, rainfall has nowhere to go but run off.

"Runoff is likely going to start much quicker and lead to those flooding impacts quicker," Greulich said.

By late Tuesday, rain had started in parts of the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles. Parts of Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa were under flood watches, with flooding possible through at least Thursday.

Baja California residents were 'lucky'

Hurricane Polo pummeled Baja California Sur with powerful winds and rain as it made landfall.

After Polo passed over the small fishing town of Puerto San Carlos on the Baja California peninsula, residents waded among downed trees through ankle-high water that flooded some homes. Seeing their roughened community largely intact brought relief to those who had prepared for the worst.

Sponsor Message

Shopkeeper Elbia María Bachomo, 40, picked through furniture strewn through her home. She and her three children had gathered their clothes quickly and left for a shelter Monday as water began flooding into their home. Her husband was out on the water fishing for sardines when Polo hit. Bachomo said he was fortunate to escape alive.

"I thought, 'Oh no, what are we going to come back to? We will be left with nothing.' But we were lucky," she said.

Hundreds of people were in shelters Tuesday in Baja California Sur, but they were expected to return to their homes.

Meanwhile, the hurricane center reported Tropical Storm Rachel was moving parallel to Mexico's coast Tuesday and was expected to become a hurricane soon. The storm was about 300 miles (482.8 kilometers) west-southwest of Lazaro Cardenos with maximum sustained winds of 70 mph (112.6 kph). It was moving northwest at 13 mph (20 kph).

In the central Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Nolo was starting to slow Tuesday but still threatened dangerous conditions for parts of Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, a marine conservation area. The storm moved northward after drenching parts of the Big Island over the weekend.

Pacific storm activity has been above average this year. That is consistent with El Niño years.

title: Powerful Hurricane Polo drenches Mexico's coast as Nolo takes aim at Hawaii
content:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — Residents along Mexico's west coast stacked sandbags to fortify beachfront shops and evacuated their homes, while Hawaii's Big Island and Maui braced for potentially catastrophic flooding, as separate hurricanes swirled in the Pacific on Thursday.

Nolo became a hurricane in the Pacific Ocean on Thursday night and was expected to strengthen while turning toward the Big Island, the National Hurricane Center said. Forecasters warned that the Big Island could see rainfall totals of 15 to 30 inches (38 to 76 centimeters), with higher amounts possible through Saturday. The island of Maui also could be hit with life-threatening floods, the hurricane center said.

Meanwhile, heavy rains from powerful Hurricane Polo could cause torrential flooding and landslides in Mexico, according to the U.S. hurricane center. In the port city of Lázaro Cárdenas, seawater already swept through homes Thursday and left wooden planks and furniture strewn on the streets.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Polo has fluctuated between Category 4 and 5, both major-hurricane strength. It was expected to regain Category 5 status on Friday, then gradually weaken Friday night and Saturday, the hurricane center said.

After skirting Mexico's coast, Polo was expected to move farther out to sea Thursday night and Friday before hooking back toward land to the north on Saturday.

The series of powerful storms comes as the weather phenomenon El Niño prompts major environmental shifts across the world, fueling drought in some areas and flooding in others. El Niño traditionally dampens the Atlantic hurricane season, while it tends to rev up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific with moist air and little wind shear.

Hawaii has been battered this year by major flooding in the spring, an earthquake and two other hurricanes since mid-August.

Advertisement Advertisement

"In my 20 years of experience here, I've never seen three hurricane watches for the islands in the same year," said John Bravender of the National Weather Service in Honolulu.

Polo could trigger flooding and mudslides in Mexico

Mexican authorities were opening shelters and clearing people from beaches, while coastal residents tried to protect businesses from getting swept away. People in high-risk areas were being evacuated, though authorities didn't immediately say how many.

Much of the worry from locals comes from hurricanes in past years that devastated cities along the Pacific coast. Hurricane Otis in 2023 unexpectedly plunged Acapulco into turmoil for weeks.

"So many people said it wouldn't happen and then it did. After that, you're left on edge," said Gonzalo Ramírez, a bartender in the city.

Advertisement Advertisement

Polo posed the biggest threat to Guerrero and Michoacán, neighboring states in southwest Mexico that share a long coastline scattered with small ports, tourist towns and fishing villages. Much of the area is marked by poverty, and residents routinely complain they are left to fend for themselves during natural disasters.

Mexican authorities have deployed 15,000 security personnel across the coast and suspended schools.

In Lázaro Cárdenas, a port city in Michoacán that was hit with high surf, locals and government officials were clearing out piles of wooden planks from a number of destroyed ramadas and shoveling thick mud coating much of the town.

Alicia Contreras said the walls and roof of her restaurant had been severely damaged by 15-foot (4.5-meter) waves. As officers and family helped pick through the damaged house, Contreras worried how she would economically recover.

Advertisement Advertisement

"This is huge because we have no other source of income. Now we're just surviving," Contreras said.

Nolo could flood parts of Hawaii still recovering from other storms

While the Big Island is expected to bear the brunt of Nolo, its full path remains uncertain, according to Bravender, the weather service's warning coordination meteorologist in Hawaii.

Most concerning, he said Thursday, is that the heaviest rain is likely to fall over the same southeastern region of the Big Island hit in August by Hurricane Lala and where grounds are still wet from additional precipitation.

"There are several communities that were isolated, flooded, roads that were washed out," he said. "It's that same area that is most under threat," Bravender said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Hawaii officials told residents to put together emergency kits and the governor issued an emergency proclamation, activating more than 230 Hawaii National Guard members. Schools were closed for the rest of the week.

Hawaiian Electric, the state's primary utility, said crews that had been helping restore power in Kauai after this month's Hurricane Lowell would return to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in preparation for the coming storm.

Odalys and Fay are not near land

A third storm in the Pacific, Hurricane Odalys, was centered far from land, roughly 1,110 miles (1,785 kilometers) west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico's Baja California peninsula.

In the northern Atlantic Ocean, Tropical Storm Fay re-formed early Thursday, the U.S. hurricane center said. It was nearly 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) west-southwest of the Azores.

Advertisement Advertisement

Tropical Storm Gonzalo formed in the Atlantic Ocean late Thursday, about 190 miles (306 kilometers) southeast of the Cape Verde islands off the coast of West Africa. The U.S. hurricane center said that if it stays on its current track, the storm will pass near or over portions of the islands Friday.

___

Aoun Angueira reported from San Diego. Associated Press journalists John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City and Jeriel Vargas Ambriz in Lázaro Cárdena, Mexico, contributed to this report.

title: 'Extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo intensifies to rare category 5 storm
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
Hurricane Polo, a large storm off the coast of Mexico, has been downgraded to category 4 but remains "very powerful", the US National Hurricane Center said.

The Pacific hurricane, one of the strongest of the season, was projected to head towards the coast of south-western Mexico, bringing intense wind and rain, though was not expected to make landfall.

A Hurricane Hunter aircraft, operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), flew into the storm on Tuesday and recorded sustained wind speeds near 180 mph (285 km/h), with stronger gusts.

The slow-moving storm is being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon.

It was previously a category 5 storm - the highest level on the scale - but was downgraded to category 4 on Wednesday morning.

Forecasters said that the storm was expected to fluctuate in intensity over the next few days.

title: How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias
author: Willa Rubin
content:
How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias

toggle caption i RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP via Getty Images

Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the season, is expected to make landfall on Friday evening near the Alabama Gulf Coast and Florida panhandle.

Days ago, the oil industry around the U.S. Gulf Coast started preparing. A segment of the nation's oil infrastructure — like oil rigs and platforms — operates in the region, although the majority of it is further west, towards western Louisiana and Texas.

Although oil experts are not anticipating major disruptions, oil companies have been taking precautions. Shell and BP have evacuated personnel from offshore facilities close to the storm's path, mainly deepwater platforms. Chevron has evacuated offshore drilling rigs close to the storm's path, and plans to redeploy them once the storm has passed.

Sponsor Message

In an emailed statement, Exxon told NPR they are "closely monitoring the weather. Operations are normal."

But so far, the storm seems like it will skirt most facilities. The storm's path "could be worse," said Debnil Chowdhury, head of Americas refining at S&P Global Energy. After all, the storm is heading east, and not west, toward where the bulk of oil operations — like refineries — are located.

The storm is "making a swooping turn, almost just to the east of where the most significant infrastructure is," said Bryan Domangue, the Gulf of America region director for the federal Marine Minerals Administration, who oversees offshore oil and natural gas production. "At this point, it's swept just a little south of some of our major deepwater oil and gas facilities, and then it's hugging the eastern boundary of where the infrastructure is."

He added that in addition to evacuating people who work on oil rigs and platforms, which are normal storm precautions, oil operators are doing things like shutting off safety valves below the ocean floor, and moving mobile drilling facilities when possible.

Of course, it's not unprecedented for the oil industry to face hurricanes. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita , in 2005, remain some of the most destructive in the oil and gas industry's history. Nearly 3,000 platforms were in the path of the storms and Katrina destroyed 47 platforms. Other, more recent, hurricanes have not been as destructive but have halted production or reduced capacity — such as Hurricane Francine in 2024 , Hurricane Ida in 2021 , and Hurricane Harvey in 2017 .

Sponsor Message

Another risk is what would happen if the storm became severe enough to make refineries — which are on land — go offline, analysts told NPR. If a hurricane knocks out the power, or if a refinery floods, it can take a while to get running again. It's more complicated than restarting an oil rig or mobile drilling operations.

"Restarting these things is like starting up an old car," said Carl Larry, a manager at Enverus, an energy data and research provider, even if the shutdown is short. "If you did anything in the world, anything in your life, 24/7, stop doing it for one day," he continued, "you're going to have the shakes."

He says, this is because refineries are vast and complex. They boil oil down into molecules that are turned into diesel, gasoline, or natural gas liquids like propane. Pipelines carry crude oil in and refined products out. And they have to be heated. "Every one of those little steps is built on power that's generated through the facility on a constant 24/7 basis," Larry said. If that power is switched off, the process takes time to restart.

There are two significant refineries on the hurricane's path — the Chevron Pascagoula location and the Vertex Alabama refinery. Representatives of these refineries did not return requests for comment about their storm preparations, but Ross Allen, a spokesperson for Chevron, told NPR that generally speaking, refineries prepare for storms by trying to mitigate flood risk.

Chowdhury of S&P Global Energy said these two refineries "account for about 2.5% of total U.S. refining capacity and about 5% the Gulf Coast refining capacity. And Pascagoula specifically is very important to supplying airports throughout the southeast."

While those numbers may not sound big, the global supply of diesel and gas is short, due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. So every little bit counts. American refineries are operating at 92.7% capacity, refining about 17 million barrels of crude a day.

title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
Verified footage shows one side of a cathedral in Penonomé collapsed due to the shaking, as well as one of its spires.

Another video showed a local hotel had almost completely collapsed.

Ricardo Brown, who lives in the southern Herrera province, told news agency Reuters that the earthquake had damaged several homes in his neighbourhood of Las Minas.

"We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked and we're afraid it could fall on us," the 74-year-old said.

The full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, though several large aftershocks were also reported near the initial earthquake, potentially complicating the situation on the surface.

The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.

Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km from the epicentre, and were seen taking to the streets or sitting in nearby parks until the shaking had ceased.

Damage in the capital appears to be limited to that caused by debris falling from roofs.

Panama's President José Raúl Mulino said his entire government was mobilising in response to the earthquake, adding: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder."

title: Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
author: Mamita Bhandari Diaa Hadid
content:
Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?

toggle caption i Skanda Gautam/AFP/via Getty Images

KATHMANDU, Nepal — On a recent September day, Sumana Shrestha Amatya stood alongside other protesters in the Nepali capital, urging the government to work faster to find their loved ones, trapped inside hydropower plants since flash floods devastated miles of a river valley in late August.

Amatya says she hasn't heard from officials about her husband, Sunil, a geologist. Still, she acknowledged the scale of the disaster that the government was grappling with: "It was like a Himalayan tsunami."

It's a description other Nepalis have used for the events of Aug. 26, when a glacier and its bedrock spanning more than 3,800 feet in width collapsed into a river valley, some 4,000 feet below.

Sponsor Message

That triggered 30-foot-high waves of boulders, water and ice that surged for miles downstream. It swept away a multistory border building and some 70 bridges and miles of highway, and buried 12 hydropower plants under mud and boulders along the Trishuli River, which was badly impacted by the floods.

Some 1,400 bodies have been recovered in Nepal, and more than 5,000 remain unaccounted for.

The dead and missing include 121 people who were trapped in hydropower plants, according to Brig. Gen. Subas Jung Thapa of the Nepali army, which is leading rescue efforts. He spoke in early September.

It took days just to find the power plants under the mud. It was like "a bomb's gone off," said Arnold Dix, a tunneling expert helping with rescue efforts. "It's removed the power stations from the surface, like they're just not there." Only three men were found alive in the plants since rescue efforts began.

Did hydropower projects add to the risk?

It is those hydropower plants that have received the most scrutiny in regional media since the floods, with experts reviving questions about whether developers had properly assessed the risks of building them in the Himalayas.

"We need to understand what is happening now in Nepal can happen in other parts of the Himalayas," says C.P. Rajendran, an Indian geoscientist who has been critical of big construction works in the Himalayas. (Rajendran, like many Indians, uses initials for his first name.)

Sponsor Message

Critics have also focused on the role of international institutions like the World Bank, which has long supported some of these hydropower projects and their associated dams.

They include one of the biggest hydropower projects in the river basin, known as the Upper Trishuli-1, which cost Nepal over half a billion dollars. It was backed by about $300 million in loans and equity by two arms of the World Bank.

The Upper-Trishuli-1 was under construction. Now it's under the mud. Thapa of the Nepali army said in his press briefing that he estimated some 50 people were trapped inside. On Wednesday, the Kathmandu Post reported the bodies of five men were recovered from the plant.

"Why did it have to happen in the first place?" asked Parineeta Dandekar, an expert on rivers who has written critically about these projects for the advocacy group South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People.

Dandekar accuses the World Bank of producing a flawed risk assessment report for the project from the get-go. Its many omissions, Dandekar says, included ignoring "the cumulative disaster risk that can happen after having so many projects across the same river."

Experts say the Trishuli river basin has 36 hydro power projects — including the dozen now under the mud.

Dandekar says the constant blasting of mountains to build these projects, including for miles-long tunnels, has its own impact.

It's a region where earthquakes and landslides are common, and where climate change is causing its glaciers to melt more rapidly, making them — and their slopes — more unstable. Initial analysis suggests global warming exacerbated the melting of the glacier that snapped off in August, triggering flash floods.

There's no clear evidence that the construction of these projects had a role in causing the severity of the Aug. 26 disaster. But experts like geoscientist Rajendran say construction has caused damage in other communities where hydropower projects are being built, including damaging mountain springs, causing homes to crack and even landslides.

Sponsor Message

In this case, though, says Dipak Gyawali, a hydropower engineer with the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology, "compared to the tectonic forces at play that caused this event, dynamiting is minuscule. This is almost nothing. It's like scratching your skin."

But he and other experts said developers were not seriously investigating the risk caused by so many projects built in the same zone. "These risks have to be properly studied and assessed. Unfortunately, they have not been," Gyawali said.

Retired Indian ambassador Shyam Saran, who served as the Indian prime minister's special envoy for climate change, says developers typically look at risks that could be triggered by their project, alongside environmental risks to it, and they appear safe. "But if you do actually a cumulative environmental impact assessment of the whole river system," he says, "then a different picture emerges."

And the Trishuli river "is a really high-risk area to build [hydropower] dams, says Austin Lord of the Stimson Center, who works on disaster risk reduction in the Himalayan region at the Stimson Center. In events exacerbated by climate change, there's been deadly flooding three years in a row in the Trishuli basin. In 2024, it was extreme rainfall. In 2025, a glacial lake burst. This year, a glacier snapped off.

A pre-flood warning

Days before the August flood, Lord and others authored a paper warning that the area was particularly vulnerable to glacial lakes bursting. "Recurring landslides, and prolonged closures," they wrote, "had all highlighted its vulnerability."

In a statement, the World Bank told NPR that the hydropower plant's design reflected assessments that looked at the risk of flooding and landslides using evidence available when the assessment was made in 2018. The statement said that as more information becomes available about the August floods, "the World Bank Group will consider any implications for risk assessment, monitoring, early warning and emergency response measures in hydropower projects."

Sponsor Message

Another major funder for the Upper Trishuli-1 was the Asian Development Bank, which loaned $60 million for the project. In 2024, independent experts who visited the site reported that no climate resilience assessment was undertaken. They described that as a "significant gap." The bank did not immediately respond to NPR's question as to whether that assessment was ultimately undertaken.

Arnold Dix, the tunneling expert, defended the hydropower plants' construction. "They were built properly to start with," he said, noting the underground infrastructure, including tunnels, was still intact. He said the collapsing glacier that triggered the August flash floods was an unforeseen new threat that "will change the way we do the designs of the power station."

Rethinking hydropower in the Himalayas

Advocates say they hope this devastating flood might prompt a rethink of how hydropower is constructed across the Himalayas. Reuters reported in 2025 that China and India, the world's most populous countries, have built 68 major dams in the Himalayas and another 101 are in the pipeline.

Most prominently, China is constructing one of the world's largest dams and hydropower plants in Tibet, costing around $170 billion. It's estimated that it will provide power to 300 million people.

In July, Chinese geologists reported that the dam is being constructed over an active fault line, risking the integrity of the project's infrastructure. Chinese officials have maintained that the project is safe and that they had considered downstream communities.

"If something happens, it is going to be a monumental disaster," says retired ambassador Saran. He says Chinese authorities have assured their neighbors that the hydro project is safe. "But as we see," he says, "those precautions which supposedly had been taken don't mean very much when you have nature's fury to deal with."

That Chinese hydropower plant and dam is being built some 30 miles from the border of the Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, according to the state's Chief Minister Pema Khandu. In 2025 statements to the media, he described two possible threats: It could hold back much of the water that presently passes downstream, and it could inundate downstream areas, whether by negligence, design or natural disaster.

Sponsor Message

For now, India's strategy appears to be building its own dam in Arunachal Pradesh in case China releases — perhaps deliberately — enormous quantities of water, as Chief Minister Khandu suggested in June last year to the outlet, Press Trust of India. "Setting aside the military threat from China, it seems to me that this is a far bigger issue than anything else. It is going to cause an existential threat to our tribes and our livelihoods. It is quite serious because China could even use this as a sort of water bomb," Khandu was quoted as saying.

Many in the local community have opposed the dam, even damaging bridges to prevent surveyors from entering the area. On Wednesday, local media reported that India's premier criminal investigation agency filed a case against Bhanu Tatak, the adviser to a group resisting the hydropower project, accusing her of illegally taking funds from foreign entities. She's previously said the Indian state has been trying to find ways to stop her advocacy.

Rajendran, the geoscientist, said both China and India needed to undertake smaller projects that are less politically attractive but less disruptive to people and their environments. "The kind of construction they are doing," he says, "it might happen probably 25 years later, or maybe 30 or 40 years later, but there will be a huge tragedy

Bhandari reported from Kathmandu. Hadid reported from Mumbai.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

title: Hurricane Isaias rapidly intensifies as evacuation orders expand to several cities
author: Julian Atienza
content:
Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday as a dangerous Category 2 storm, lashing the northern Gulf Coast with destructive winds and life-threatening storm surge.

The powerful storm made landfall at 9:30 p.m. ET near Destin, Florida, with sustained winds of 105 mph and an estimated minimum central pressure of 971 mb as it moved north at 19 mph.

More than 30 million people across Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Georgia are expected to experience the worst of Isaias' impacts, while rain from the storm’s remnants will spread across more than 15 states in the eastern U.S. after landfall this weekend.

HURRICANE ISAIAS THREATENS MORE THAN COASTLINE WITH IMPACTS TO PUSH INLAND ACROSS SOUTH

Isaias was previously a Category 3 hurricane, but as of the 8 p.m. NHC advisory, the dangerous storm has slightly weakened to a Category 2.

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) said weather conditions are deteriorating rapidly and urged Gulf Coast residents to seek shelter immediately.

Rain has been lashing parts of the coast for several hours ahead of the storm.

Water levels are rising around Panama City and Apalachicola, Florida, while a storm surge blowout is underway in Mobile Bay, Alabama.

Water levels in Panama City Beach, Florida, recently reached 5.4 feet above the average high tide level.

A Flash Flood Emergency was issued on Friday night for Fort Walton Beach, Florida and Destin, Florida amid the threat of life-threatening flooding.

TROPICAL STORM RACHEL TARGETS THE WEST COAST WITH FLOODING RAIN AND GUSTY WINDS

Meanwhile, hurricane-force wind gusts were already battering the Gulf Coast, with officials reporting gusts of 102 mph at Pensacola City Hall.

The Storm Prediction Center has issued a Tornado Watch effective until 9:00 p.m. ET (8:00 p.m. CT) for the Florida Panhandle, extreme southern Georgia, and southeast Alabama.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey and Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp have declared states of emergency ahead of the storm.

In a Friday news conference, DeSantis urged residents to follow evacuation orders due to storm surge.

"The surge is really what puts a lot of people's lives in jeopardy if they haven't heeded evacuation orders and does the most significant damage from these storms," DeSantis said.

"Preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds should be rushed to completion in the warning area," the NHC said.

Over a dozen Florida and Alabama counties have canceled school through the end of the week, and multiple colleges have closed their campuses.

HOW ARE HURRICANES RATED?

Meanwhile, evacuation orders have been issued across parts of Alabama and Florida, including Dauphin Island, Alabama, and Okaloosa and Escambia counties in Florida.

Mandatory evacuation orders have also been issued in Walton County, Florida.

Orange Beach, Alabama, has also issued mandatory evacuations.

"In anticipation of the expected impacts from Tropical Storm Isaias, the cities of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach are encouraging all non‑residents, and residents living in low-lying, flood prone areas to voluntarily evacuate," a statement from city officials said. "City officials urge all individuals who are not permanent residents to leave the area immediately and relocate to a safer location."

Both Shell and Chevron have instituted shut-in production procedures across five of their offshore oil facilities in the Gulf and removed non-essential workers, respectively.

BP said it was also removing non-essential personnel and securing offshore facilities Thursday. ExxonMobil operations are currently normal, but said they are monitoring the forecast closely.

HURRICANE ISAIAS CHURNS IN GULF AS OIL RIGS PREPARE FOR POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS CONDITIONS

Hurricane Isaias strengthened from Tropical Storm Isaias late Wednesday night.

WHAT’S THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A TROPICAL DEPRESSION, TROPICAL STORM AND HURRICANE?

Isaias rapidly intensified from a tropical storm into a Category 1 hurricane, with winds increasing by 40 mph in just six hours between Wednesday afternoon and late Wednesday night.

Hurricane Isaias' expected impacts

Tropical weather advisories have expanded well inland, across parts of eastern Mississippi, Alabama and southwestern Georgia.

A Hurricane Warning is in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf County Line in Florida.

Tropical Storm Warnings are in effect just outside Isaias’ forecast cone, bookended by the Jefferson-Plaquemines Parish line in Louisiana to the west and the Aucilla River in Florida to the east.

LATEST FROM FOX WEATHER HURRICANE SPECIALIST BRYAN NORCROSS

A Storm Surge Warning for life-threatening surge is in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Suwannee River in Florida's Big Bend region.

"There is a danger of life-threatening inundation, from rising water moving inland from the coastline, during the next 36 hours in the indicated locations," the NHC said.

New forecast data from the NHC now calls for up to 9 feet of life-threatening storm surge from the Alabama-Florida to Grayton Beach, Florida.

FOX WEATHER JOINS THE HURRICANE HUNTERS ON CRITICAL RECON MISSION INTO TROPICAL STORM ISAIAS

The Lower Mobile Bay could see up to 5 feet of surge.

Heavy rain began Friday morning, with flash flooding, damaging wind gusts, storm surge and even tornadoes possible as the storm comes ashore.

Heavy rain quickly picked up throughout the day on Friday from Louisiana to Florida and will last through Saturday. FOX Weather Hurricane Specialist Bryan Norcross said some of the strongest impacts will arrive ahead of landfall.

"Bad weather will arrive well in advance of the center, which will cross the coast mid to late evening on the current schedule," Norcross said.

HOW TO WATCH FOX WEATHER

"Thunderstorms are likely along the I-10 corridor this afternoon with the worst weather arriving in the evening."

Norcross noted most of the storm's most impactful weather will most likely be on the right side of the storm's center.

NOAA's Weather Prediction Center (WPC) has issued a Level 3 out of 4 flash flood risk for Mobile, Alabama, and the Florida Panhandle west of Panama City. A Level 2 risk includes Atlanta and Montgomery, Alabama, and eventually shifts inland into Saturday to include the Carolinas and Tennessee Valley.

7 FACTS YOU SHOULD KNOW ABOUT FLASH FLOODS

"Rainfall estimates currently show 6 to 10 inches with localized higher amounts of up to 15 inches of rain, which will lead to flash and urban flooding and eventually river flooding," the FOX Forecast Center said.

NOAA's Storm Prediction Center (SPC) has issued a Level 2 out of 5 risk of severe weather for Saturday for tornadoes as the storm's outer bands come ashore. The greatest tornado threat covers parts of southeastern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and have now been expanded across southern and Central Georgia into southern South Carolina, including Columbia.

TROPICAL STORM ISAIAS CHURNS IN GULF AS OIL RIGS PREPARE FOR POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS CONDITIONS

The system is expected to move inland quickly with heavy rain spreading across the Southeast Saturday, triggering a broad Level 2 flash flood risk from some places along the Mississippi River to the Southeast coast.

This area stretches from Tallahassee north into western North Carolina, to the Southeast coast and into the Tennessee Valley.

"The heaviest rain will be across the Carolinas, where 5-8 inches of rain will fall from Charleston to Wilmington," the FOX Forecast Center said.

A High Wind Warning has been issued across parts of northern Alabama, northern Georgia and Western North Carolina beginning Saturday afternoon.

Atlanta could see wind gusts up to 60 mph Saturday.

Rain will spread into the Northeast by Sunday, creating a flash flood risk across parts of the Interstate 95 corridor.

Isaias became the Atlantic season’s first hurricane late Wednesday.

El Niño-driven wind shear has caused a record-slow start to the Atlantic hurricane season, with Isaias becoming the latest first hurricane to form since the satellite era began in 1966.

This story is developing. Check back frequently for updates.

title: Hurricane Polo makes Baja landfall, headed for a 2nd in Mexico
author: Abc News
content:
Polo slammed the Mexican mainland after making landfall in Baja California.

Hurricane Polo makes 2nd landfall in Mexico as Category 1 storm

A man carries items through floodwater past downed electric lines after the passing of Hurricane Polo in Puerto San Carlos, Baja California Sur state, Mexico, September 29, 2026.

A man carries items through floodwater past downed electric lines after the passing of Hurricane Polo in Puerto San Carlos, Baja California Sur state, Mexico, September 29, 2026.

A man carries items through floodwater past downed electric lines after the passing of Hurricane Polo in Puerto San Carlos, Baja California Sur state, Mexico, September 29, 2026.

A man carries items through floodwater past downed electric lines after the passing of Hurricane Polo in Puerto San Carlos, Baja California Sur state, Mexico, September 29, 2026.

Hurricane Polo made a second landfall along the northwest coast of Mexico on Tuesday after making its initial landfall in Baja California overnight.

On Tuesday afternoon, Polo slammed the mainland of Mexico as a Category 1 storm, coming ashore east of Guaymas and bringing high winds and heavy rains.

Polo made its first landfall overnight along the Baja California Peninsula near Las Barrancas as a Category 2 hurricane, packing dangerous winds of 96 to 110 mph.

A man carries items through floodwater past downed electric lines after the passing of Hurricane Polo in Puerto San Carlos, Baja California Sur state, Mexico, September 29, 2026. Eduardo Verdugo/AP Photo

After making landfall around 11 p.m. local time Monday, Polo was downgraded to a Category 1 storm as it trekked across the Baja before taking aim at the Sonora region of mainland Mexico.

There were no immediate reports of major damage or injuries.

Polo formed into a Pacific hurricane on Sept. 20, one of three hurricanes to develop in the Pacific at the same time.

Tracking Polo and other tropical disturbances in the Pacific. ABC News

Near-record levels of moisture are coming in from the Pacific, aided by strong flow from Polo.

The hurricane's remnants will eventually merge later Tuesday with an existing storm system and supercharge moisture across a large swath of the United States.

Tracking the accumulation of rain through Thursday. ABC News

More than 30 million people on Tuesday across a dozen states from California and Texas to Iowa are under a flood watch.

Overnight, multiple flash flood warnings were in effect across Utah and Arizona.

Latest flash flooding alerts. ABC News

Zion National Park saw near-record flooding along the Virgin River and Heaps Canyon as a flash flood wave moved through on Monday night.

Water rescues were made on Monday evening in Bullhead City, Arizona, after a vehicle got trapped in floodwaters.

title: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama
author: Bill Chappell
content:
At least 4 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama

toggle caption i Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage and power outages wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least four people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed.

Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland.

One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office.

"The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email.

A person also died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a room, according to Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons. Four others were hospitalized in the same incident. Many people use generators when they lose connection to the electricity grid.

toggle caption i Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham.

Sponsor Message

"We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence."

A fourth death was confirmed by Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey's office, which told NPR that a person died in Barbour County, southeast of Montgomery. They did not provide details about the circumstances.

More than 390,000 people across the state and Florida were without power as of Sunday morning. At least 95% of outages across the state are expected to be restored by midnight, Alabama Power said on Sunday.

In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference.

The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners.

"Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges.

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Florida Power & Light Company said it hopes to have power restored to 95% of those impacted by Isaias by end of day Monday.

Sponsor Message

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin.

Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama.

"Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county," tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service."

But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as the Florida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast.

On Sunday, there were tornado warnings in North Carolina, as well as high risk of flooding. Other parts of the rest of the East Coast, including Virginia, also saw heavy rain.

NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report.

title: Homes and bridges swept away as fresh floods hit Nepal
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said.

Officials say they have rescued 95 people, including nine foreigners, along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing.

A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex.

Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing.

Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar.

More than 200 homes were damaged and more than 650 people were impacted by the flood, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.

Some settlements have been completely cut off and are now only accessible by air, a local official told The Kathmandu Post.

Nepal's army said it had mobilised four helicopters for search and rescue operations.

Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies.

Ganesh Karki, a resident of Jagatbagar, told The Kathmandu Post that he and others took shelter about 500m (0.3 miles) uphill in a nearby forest after receiving a warning call about the flood early in the morning.

"We never imagined a flood of this size," he said. "The water surged for about 15 minutes and then stopped repeatedly throughout the morning. We are afraid to return home at night."

The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the disaster management authority said.

Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said.

Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location."

However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August.

What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche.

Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood.

"Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said.

"We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet."

The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where an avalanche of rock and ice in August caused floods along the Nepal-Tibet border. The avalanche happened near the peak of Lantang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas. Hundreds of people were killed in those floods.

Nepal is prone to disasters, from earthquakes to landslides and floods, as a result of the unpredictable natural environment in the Himalayas.

Experts say climate change, which is making glaciers melt faster, is likely raising the risk of such disasters, leaving local communities increasingly vulnerable.

title: Isaias strengthens into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season
author: Bill Chappell
content:
Isaias strengthens into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season

toggle caption i National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration/National Oceanic and Atmospheric

Isaias is now the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 — and it's spinning toward the southeastern U.S., according to the National Hurricane Center. Isaias strengthened into a hurricane Wednesday night and is forecast to approach the northern Gulf Coast on Friday afternoon, with landfall possible late Friday or early Saturday.

As of Thursday afternoon, Isaias was about 355 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River, moving east-northeast at 10 mph. The storm's maximum sustained winds were 85 mph, the hurricane center said.

Sponsor Message

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey has declared a state of emergency for 40 counties; Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis did the same for 25 counties. In Florida, mandatory or voluntary evacuation orders are in effect for parts of seven counties as of midday Thursday.

Isaias doesn't have a classic hurricane shape; instead, it leans like an italicized O. And that likely means trouble for Florida, DeSantis said in an update Thursday afternoon, noting that hurricanes' worst impacts are often on their northeastern quadrant.

"The issue with this storm is it's a very eastside-heavy storm," DeSantis said, noting that forecasts predict landfall near Mobile Bay and the Florida-Alabama line — meaning much of Florida's panhandle could bear the brunt of the storm. He said that area should prepare for power outages.

When the storm does arrive, it will drench ground that's already been soaked by recent heavy rainfall.

"We are saturated" in that area of Florida, DeSantis said.

A wide swath of the Gulf Coast is under a hurricane warning, from Ocean Springs, Miss., to the area around Mexico Beach in Florida. Storm surge alerts cover an even larger area. If the storm surge's peak coincides with high tide, it could hit the coastline from Ocean Springs to Indian Pass, Fla., with 5 to 7 feet of water.

Sponsor Message

Describing Florida's preparations, DeSantis said more than 6,000 utility linemen and restoration workers are standing by. The Florida National Guard expects to have approximately 5,000 personnel available to help, he said.

toggle caption i National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration/Screenshot by NPR

Isaias ends an extraordinary four-month run with no other Atlantic hurricanes since the season began on June 1.

"While we anticipated a well below-average season this year, it's certainly been surprising to see just how quiet it has been," Philip Klotzbach, a research scientist in the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State University, told NPR.

Since 1851, only three hurricane seasons on record have had no hurricanes through Oct. 7, Klotzbach said – though he noted that some early storms might have been missed in the era before aircraft reconnaissance or satellites.

The dearth is widely attributed to a Super El Niño climate pattern that has made powerful ocean storms less likely in the Atlantic and much more likely in the Pacific. In an average year, the Atlantic would have had at least five hurricanes by now, according to the National Hurricane Center, citing data from recent decades.

The center predicts Isaias could bring up to 10 inches of rain to some areas, with 3 to 7 inches possible from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle over the weekend.

Isaias is expected to turn toward the Northeast over Thursday and Friday; the hurricane center said forecast models are somewhat divided over the exact timing of those shifts, which would determine where the storm makes landfall.

After becoming a tropical storm on Tuesday, Isaias moved over a part of the Gulf of Mexico where conditions are very favorable for intensification, with sea surface temperatures around 87 degrees. Such warm ocean water helps tropical storms build strength and draw in moisture, adding to their potential rainfall. Because of those conditions, recent forecasts have boosted predictions about the storm's power.

Warmer sea surface temperatures are linked to human-caused climate change, a critical factor in making hurricanes larger and more likely to bring intense winds and rainfall when they make landfall.

Sponsor Message

El Niño's storm-inhibiting effects aren't as strong in the Gulf of Mexico as they are in the tropical Atlantic, Klotzbach said. The new hurricane, he added, formed with the help of a cyclonic "gyre" system that can generate storms on either side of Central America. It's responsible for both Isaias in the Atlantic and for Tropical Depression 20E in the Pacific.

A potentially positive aspect of the forecast is that Isaias is expected to move quickly over land after making landfall, rather than hovering over already-inundated areas.

"Isaias will be moving quickly as it comes onshore, which should hopefully reduce the chances for catastrophic flooding," Klotzbach said. But, he adds, the storm will still bring dangerous amounts of rain.

title: Major earthquake strikes Panama—damage and injuries are expected
author: Adam Kovac
content:
Hospital personnel and patients stand outside the maternity ward of the Santo Tomas hospital, after a severe earthquake hit the country, in Panama City on October 9, 2026.

A major earthquake struck Panama on Friday afternoon, but how many people have been affected remains unclear.

The quake struck at 12:56 P.M. local time and was initially measured as an 8.0 magnitude by the U.S. Geological Survey, but that was later downgraded slightly to a 7.7. The quake struck around nine miles (14 kilometers) southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a small village in Panama’s Herrera Province. Around 4.6 million people experienced moderate to severe shaking, according to the USGS, and potentially strong aftershocks could follow.

On social media, Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino said he had given instructions to mobilize personnel, resources and aid to the area.

On supporting science journalism

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

No statistics on injuries or deaths have yet been released. The affected area has a relatively low population density.

While the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Tsunami Warning System had initially warned that the quake could pose a tsunami threat in Costa Rica, El Salvador, Peru, Mexico, Guatemala, Nicaragua, Colombia and Ecuador as well as Panama, as of Friday afternoon the alert was no longer in effect.

The threat of tsunami has likely largely receded, says USGS seismologist Susan Hough, as the quake occurred on land and happened at a relatively shallow depth.

“Because this was on land and shallow, you’re not on the seafloor, so it didn’t move the seafloor underneath the water column, and that’s what you need to generate a tsunami,” she says.

Shallow earthquakes do lead to more shaking being felt at the surface, though. USGS modeling put the likely casualties in the range of dozens to hundreds of fatalities and damages in the hundreds of millions dollars.

The U.S. embassy in Panama did warn U.S. citizens in the area to avoid damaged structures, as well as the coast, and to monitor local emergency broadcasts for updates.

Panama is located near the intersection of several major tectonic plates. To the south are the Cocos and Nazca plates, with the Caribbean plate to the north and the South American plate to the east.

“It was a shallow lateral fault, what we call strike-slip, so similar to the San Andreas,” Hough says.

While the meeting place of tectonic plates can lead to the formation of subduction zones, areas where the denser plate is forced underneath the light plate into Earth’s mantle, which can lead to powerful earthquakes as pressure builds, Hough said the subduction zones near Panama don’t meet, which is why the country usually experiences less powerful quakes.

“There’s a complicated zone of faulting that’s at that juncture, and so this earthquake was on one of those faults,” she says. “It was quite large compared to other earthquakes that have been seen in that area.”

title: Isaias strengthens into Category 2 hurricane on collision course with the Gulf Coast
author: Bill Chappell Emma Bowman
content:
Isaias pummels the Gulf Coast, and plows through Alabama

toggle caption i Octavio Jones/AP

Nearly 900,000 power customers are without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia on Saturday, after Hurricane Isaias plowed into the northern Gulf Coast Friday night, according to the monitoring site PowerOutage.us.

Isaias made landfall Friday night near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane, packing 105 mph winds. It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- mercifully short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if Isaias arrived at peak high tide. Landfall took place around 8:30 p.m. local time, according to the National Hurricane Center, roughly two hours before high tide in Destin.

Sponsor Message

Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. But threats of widespread flash floods and wind damage remain. Rainfall totals over the weekend could reach 4 to 8 inches in parts of Alabama, Florida and Georgia, with up to 15 inches possible in some areas.

Isaias is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which has until now been dampened by a strong El Nino, a naturally occurring climate pattern. It is the first hurricane since 2024 to hit the U.S.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday evening warned residents in the hurricane's path and beyond to prepare for heavy rain and potential tornadoes.

"Assume you're going to lose power," he said at a news conference.

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images

The governor earlier stressed that while well-designed buildings can withstand high winds, floodwaters present a serious threat to lives and property.

"We always say, you know, you hide from the wind, but you run from the water," DeSantis told reporters Friday morning. "When the water's rising and things are happening, it's a very, very difficult conundrum, and you do not want to be caught in that."

A hurricane warning had extended along the Gulf Coast from Ocean Springs, Miss., eastward to the area around Mexico Beach in Florida.

Sponsor Message

Flash floods are a certainty, according to Jared Perdue, the executive director of Florida's Division of Emergency Management. "The Panhandle is already saturated from rainfall," he said at Friday morning's press conference alongside DeSantis. "This storm will bring heavy amounts of rain … there will be flash flooding, there will be localized flooding."

DeSantis said that some 16,000 utility workers were standing by to help restore electricity service. The Florida National Guard readied approximately 5,000 personnel available to help the recovery effort, he said.

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images

In the Florida Panhandle, many schools and commercial airports were shut down, and mandatory or voluntary evacuation orders were in effect for parts of seven counties as of Friday morning. In Alabama, Gov. Kay Ivey declared a state of emergency for 40 counties; DeSantis did the same for 25 counties.

It has been more than 100 years since the Atlantic got its first hurricane of the season this late, as a "Super El Niño" weather pattern has disrupted the ability of cyclones to form. But the pattern has done less to affect storm formation in the Gulf, where very warm water has served as fuel for storms like Isaias.

Warm ocean water helps tropical storms build strength and draw in moisture, adding to their potential rainfall. Warmer sea surface temperatures are also linked to human-caused climate change, a critical factor in making hurricanes larger and more likely to bring intense winds and rainfall when they make landfall.

title: Hurricane Isaias strengthens to Category 2 as Gulf Coast braces for landfall
content:
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., around 9:30 p.m. ET Friday as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, the National Hurricane Center said. It was the first hurricane of an unusually quiet Atlantic season. At least four people have died, two in Florida and two in Alabama, officials said.

The storm weakened quickly as it moved inland. As of 5 a.m. ET Saturday, it was a post-tropical storm with 35 mph winds about 25 miles south-southwest of Montgomery, Ala., moving north at 14 mph. It is expected to cross Alabama into the Tennessee Valley and dissipate Sunday.

About 700,000 homes and businesses across the Southeast were without power Saturday afternoon, down from more than 900,000 that morning, according to PowerOutage.us.

The biggest threat now is rain. The NHC expects 4 to 8 inches across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and southwest Georgia through the weekend, with up to 15 inches in spots. Flash flooding and landslides are possible in the southern Appalachians.

title: Hurricane Nolo, a zig-zagging storm, threatens Hawaii with flooding rain
author: Bill Chappell Juliana Kim
content:
Hurricane Nolo, a zig-zagging storm, threatens Hawaii with flooding rains

toggle caption i NOAA/NESDIS/STAR/GOES-West

People on the Big Island of Hawaii are under a hurricane watch Friday afternoon, as Hurricane Nolo moves over the Pacific Ocean toward the Hawaiian archipelago. The alert means hurricane conditions are possible within 24 to 36 hours. By then, the storm will likely be a major hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

Nolo isn't expected to make landfall this weekend, but it has two dangerous qualities: slow movement and heavy rain. Maximum rainfall amounts from the storm in some areas could top 2 feet, forecasters say, with totals of 10 to 25 inches expected more widely.

Sponsor Message

"The time to finish preparations for significant heavy rain and flooding impacts on the Big Island is now," the NHC said in its public advisory. "Life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides are possible."

As of Friday afternoon, Nolo's maximum sustained winds were at 105 mph, making it a Category 2 storm, and it was moving at only 5 mph. It's now moving north-northeast and is expected to slow to a crawl before turning toward the west and picking up forward speed on Saturday and Sunday.

But it will continue to build strength from warm ocean waters. Over the next 72 hours, Nolo's winds could top out at 140 mph, according to the forecast discussion, making it a Category 4 storm.

toggle caption i NOAA/National Weather Service

The heaviest rains will likely fall on the Big Island's eastern and southern areas, forecasters say. Neighboring Maui is under a tropical storm watch and could see up to 10 inches of rain.

Hawaii and Maui counties have opened shelters to people and pets, according to Hawaii Public Radio, which also reports that schools and government offices began closing on Thursday in preparation for the storm.

Nolo's path over the water has been prone to sudden shifts. Earlier this week, it was heading west across open ocean when it took an abrupt right-hand turn, sending it north directly toward the Big Island.

The cyclone is the latest in a busy hurricane season in the Pacific, where warm water is feeding a powerful El Niño phenomenon that's sparking storms and reshaping weather patterns around the world. The Pacific region has already seen three Category 5 hurricanes: Genevieve, Lowell and Polo.

Sponsor Message

Nolo brings torrential rains to Hawaii weeks after the state endured flooding and wind damage from a series of natural disasters over this past year. In March, a winter storm system called a Kona low led to the worst flooding seen in Hawaii in over two decades. Then, in May, a 6.0 magnitude earthquake shook the Big Island.

In August, Hurricane Lala raked the Big Island, Maui, Oahu and Kauai at close range. And earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell pummeled Kauai and other areas.

Earlier this week, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said these four major disasters alone have damaged or destroyed about 1,290 homes. He estimated recovery efforts will cost roughly $1 billion prior to Nolo.

"We will pursue every available federal resource, use insurance and state funding responsibly and work with the Legislature to protect our people and prepare Hawaiʻi for what comes next," he said in a press release .

toggle caption i

Nolo's growth represents a reversal: Last week, forecasters declared the system was dissipating and would not merit further updates unless it regenerated — and that's precisely what it did. Days ago, the NHC renewed issuing advisories of Tropical Depression Fifteen-E and warned that it could strengthen quickly. It then became Tropical Storm Nolo before intensifying into a hurricane.

Hurricane season in Hawaii typically runs through Nov. 30.
